title: Ram Charan's ₹337 Crore Hit Just Left the Theatre — and It's Heading Straight to Your Netflix
excerpt: Peddi, the Telugu sports drama with an A.R. Rahman score and the most physically transformed Ram Charan you've ever seen, arrives on Netflix this week. Here's why NRI viewers should watch the Telugu version first.
body:
For four weeks, Ram Charan has been running — literally and metaphorically — across Indian screens as Peddi, a village hustler turned para-athlete who refuses to quit even when the world breaks his shot at glory. Now the run continues on your couch.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=noatJVfA22U

Peddi, the Telugu sports drama that has grossed ₹337 crore worldwide since its June 4 release, is arriving on Netflix this month. The South Indian language versions — Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam, and Kannada — are expected as early as this week, according to reports from 123Telugu and Bollywood Life. The Hindi dubbed version follows later, around July 30, after completing the standard eight-week theatrical window. Netflix hasn't officially confirmed the dates, but the streaming deal is done — the platform reportedly acquired the digital rights for a staggering ₹105–130 crore, one of the biggest OTT deals for a Telugu film ever.

If you've been waiting to see what the fuss is about, here's what you're getting: a raw, sweaty, unglamorous Ram Charan like you've never seen him.

Director Buchi Babu Sana — mentored by Pushpa and Rangasthalam director Sukumar — strips the RRR superstar of his movie-star polish and puts him in a nose ring, a heavy beard, and the sun-cracked skin of a village athlete who plays cricket and wrestles for cash. When a jealous rival sabotages his shot at the National Wrestling Championship, Peddi doesn't break. He reinvents himself as a para-track athlete, channeling his rage and talent into a sport he's never tried, all to put his forgotten village on the map.

"Ram Charan, in his most physically challenging role to date, brings real grit to the character." — Bollywood Life

The romance is old-school and rooted: Janhvi Kapoor plays Achiyamma, the sarpanch's daughter, bringing a quiet warmth to a film that otherwise trades in dust and adrenaline. Their chemistry won't remind you of any other pairing — it's rural, earthy, and surprisingly tender. The supporting cast is stacked: Shiva Rajkumar as the seasoned warrior figure, Jagapathi Babu, Boman Irani, Divyenndu Sharma, and Ravi Kishan all occupying their corners of a village that feels like it could swallow you whole.

And then there's the music. A.R. Rahman — yes, that A.R. Rahman — composed the songs and the background score. The first single, Chikiri Chikiri, racked up 46 million views in 24 hours and has since crossed 200 million. The soundtrack doesn't just accompany the film; it elevates it into something primal, bridging folk rhythms with Rahman's signature layered orchestration.

The numbers tell a story of their own. Peddi opened to mixed critical reviews — some found the screenplay episodic, others questioned the pacing. But audiences voted with their feet. The India net collection stands at ₹240 crore, with overseas earnings adding another ₹53 crore. After Ram Charan's last film Game Changer underperformed, Peddi feels less like a comeback and more like a declaration: the superstar is best when he's covered in mud, not sequins.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DZ-I8d9jNUP/

For NRI viewers, this is the streaming event of the week. If you're in the US, UK, Canada, or anywhere outside India with a Netflix subscription, the Telugu version lands first — and it's the version to watch. Buchi Babu Sana wrote the film in Telugu, and the performances are calibrated for that language's rhythms and textures. The Hindi dub arrives roughly four weeks later, though if you can handle subtitles, don't wait.

What to know before you press play: Peddi runs long — this is a sprawling, emotional epic, not a tight 100-minute sports film. It takes its time building the village, the rivalries, the relationships. The payoff is earned, not rushed. Come for Ram Charan's transformation. Stay for the moment the village finally sees itself on the map.

Peddi is the kind of film that reminds you why Indian cinema at its most grounded can be more thrilling than any CGI spectacle. A village, a sport, a man who won't stop running. And now it's coming straight to your screen.
